hints: Mark that the cosecant branch decreases from $+\infty$ to 1, whereas the straight line increases from 1.
Show their single intersection and explain why opposite monotonicity prevents a second root.
walkthrough: Consider the two functions $y_1 = \operatorname{cosec}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sin(x/2)}$ and $y_2 = \dfrac{1}{3}x + 1$ on the interval $0 < x \leq \pi$.
Analyze $y_1$: as $x \to 0^+$, $\sin(x/2) \to 0^+$, so $y_1 \to +\infty$. At $x = \pi$, $y_1(\pi) = \operatorname{cosec}(\pi/2) = 1$. The curve is strictly decreasing throughout $(0, \pi]$.
Analyze $y_2$: this is a straight line starting from $y = 1$ when $x = 0$ and increasing to $y_2(\pi) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + 1 \approx 2.047$ when $x = \pi$.
Compare endpoints: near $x = 0$, $y_1 > y_2$ ($+\infty > 1$), while at $x = \pi$, $y_1(\pi) = 1 < 2.047 = y_2(\pi)$.
Since $y_1$ decreases monotonically from $+\infty$ to $1$ and $y_2$ increases monotonically from $1$ to $1 + \pi/3$, their continuous graphs intersect at exactly one point in $0 < x \leq \pi$.

hints: Evaluate this expression at 1.4 and 1.6 using radians.
Give the calculated signs and invoke the sign change to establish the root bracket.
walkthrough: Define $F(x) = \operatorname{cosec}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3}x + 1\right)$, which is continuous on $[1.4, 1.6]$.
Since $F(1.4) > 0$ and $F(1.6) < 0$, there is a change of sign across the continuous interval, verifying that the root lies strictly between $1.4$ and $1.6$.

hints: For a convergent sequence, replace $x_{n+1}$ and $x_n$ by their common limit $x$.
Rearrange $\sin(x/2)=3/(x+3)$ by taking reciprocals to reproduce the equation from part (i).
walkthrough: Assume the iterative sequence $x_{n+1} = 2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{x_n + 3}\right)$ converges to a limit $x$ in $(0, \pi]$.

Set up the fixed-point equation:
$$x = 2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{x + 3}\right)$$

Divide both sides by $2$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}x = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{x + 3}\right)$$

Apply the sine function to both sides:
$$\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = \dfrac{3}{x + 3}$$

Take the reciprocal of both sides:
$$\dfrac{1}{\sin(x/2)} = \dfrac{x + 3}{3}$$

Split the fraction on the right-hand side and identify the cosecant function:
$$\operatorname{cosec}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}x + 1$$
This is the exact equation from part (i), proving that the limit of convergence is the root of the original equation.

hints: Iterate $x_{n+1}=2\sin^{-1}(3/(x_n+3))$ in radians from a value between 1.4 and 1.6.
Carry full precision into each new evaluation but display every term to 5 decimal places.
Stop only when the displayed sequence supports an unambiguous 3-decimal-place root.
walkthrough: Use the iterative formula $x_{n+1} = 2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{x_n + 3}\right)$ with starting value $x_1 = 1.5$.
Successive iterations round to $1.471$ to 3 decimal places.

State the root correct to 3 decimal places:
$$x = 1.471$$
